tone_statements.citation: Nishida, Tatsuo. 1988 [issued 1989]. On the mTsho-sna Monpa language in China [running title: The Mtsho-sna Monpa language of China and its place in the Tibeto-Burman family]. In David Bradley, Eugénie J. A. Henderson & Martine Mazaudon (eds.), Prosodic analysis and Asian linguistics: to honour R. K. Sprigg, 223-236. Pacific Linguistics C-104. Canberra: Australian National University.
tone_statements.quote: I. Voiceless series (High tone) 2. Voiced series (Low tone) [...] In the case of the tone of syllables which began with voiceless sounds, there is another type in Monpa (Mama) besides the type with the 53 tone. For instance, ' see' te55 (WrT lta-ba) stands in opposition to 'horse ' te53 (WrT rta). The conditioning for this 53/55 split is still unclear. [...] In the case of two-syllable words, several types of tone combinations might occur, but there is a tendency for them to be integrated into two main patterns, that is, a 55-53 type and a 35-53 type.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 232-233 (correspondence table 'Syllable of Cuona Monpa (Mama)' and following paragraphs, in the section on Tibetan-Monpa correspondences); see also p. 231 bottom and fn. 7 p. 235
tone_statements.summary: Cuona (Mama/Wenlang) Dakpa is a syllable-tone language with a high register (53, 55; checked ʔ53) from old voiceless/preconsonantal onsets and a low register (35; checked ʔ35) from old voiced onsets, a further lexical 53 vs 55 contrast within the high register, marginal 13/31, and disyllabic tone patterns levelled to 55-53 / 35-53 (word-level sandhi).

sources.citation: Rüfenacht, Sara & Sereina Waldis. 2020. Diachronic and areal aspects of Brokpa phonology. Himalayan Linguistics 19(1). (read for its second-hand Dakpa notes; not saved to our check folder)
sources.tag: read: notes on stress
sources.note: About Brokpa, not Dakpa; no use of the word stress. Reports second-hand that Hyslop & Tshering (2010: 12) describe voiceless word-final high vowels in Dakpa (akpu̥ 'crow', phuipu̥ 'male') and that Bodt (2012: 283) notes deletion of word-final high vowels in Thongrong Dakpa -- i.e. both inaccessible sources have Dakpa phonology sections.

sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2 Phonology (pp. 106-110) covers consonants, vowels, and sec. 2.3 'Tone and vowel length' (p. 109-110): two-way high/low tone, contrastive only after sonorants, predictable after stops; tone not marked in the paper. The words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the article. (Indirect hint only: word-final vowels dropped in normal speech, e.g. /sirp/ 'yellow' = sirpo in careful speech, p. 107-108.)
